# IAM Identity Center, Directory Service and Cognito: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=identity-federation-q010 -->
### Question 1

A company hosts an internet-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The load balancer has an HTTPS listener with a certificate. The company sells the application to business customers. Each customer's employees must sign in with that customer's corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider before any request reaches the instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Add each customer's SAML identity provider to IAM Identity Center as an identity source, and assign the web application to each customer's employees.
- Create a Cognito user pool with each customer's SAML identity provider, and add an authenticate-cognito action to a new HTTP listener on port 80.
- Create a Cognito user pool with each customer's SAML identity provider, and add an authenticate-cognito action to the rules of the existing HTTPS listener.
- Put an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API in front of the load balancer, and write a Lambda authorizer that validates the SAML assertions of each customer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Cognito user pool with each customer's SAML identity provider, and add an authenticate-cognito action to the rules of the existing HTTPS listener.

**Deciding phrases.** "corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider", "before any request reaches the instances", "LEAST development effort"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST development effort.
2. I mark the constraints: an internet-facing Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener, the corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider of each customer, and sign-in before any request reaches the instances.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a Cognito user pool with the SAML providers and an authenticate-cognito rule on the load balancer, because the load balancer can sign users in before it forwards a request.
4. I remove IAM Identity Center, because it connects one SAML identity provider at a time and serves the company's own workforce. I remove API Gateway with a Lambda authorizer, because SAML checks in a function are code to write and run.
5. Between the two user pool options the difference is the listener; the stem says the load balancer has an HTTPS listener, and the authenticate-cognito action works on HTTPS listeners only, so I keep the rule on the existing HTTPS listener.
6. Check: the user pool with the rule on the HTTPS listener meets every constraint and needs no sign-in code. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The load balancer signs users in before it forwards a request, and the action is [supported only with HTTPS listeners](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-alb-authenticate-cognito-https-only), which the stem has. The user pool accepts each customer's SAML provider and [issues JSON web tokens (JWTs)](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-saml-idp-must-support-saml-2) of its own, so the application needs no sign-in code.

**Why not.**

- "Add each customer's SAML identity provider to IAM ...": IAM Identity Center connects [only one directory or one SAML 2.0 identity provider](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-one-identity-source-at-a-time) at a time, and it serves the company's own workforce.
- "Create a Cognito user pool with each customer's ...": The authenticate-cognito action is [supported only with HTTPS listeners](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-alb-authenticate-cognito-https-only), so a rule on an HTTP listener does not sign users in.
- "Put an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API in ...": It adds code to write and run: the team builds SAML handling that the user pool and the load balancer provide without code. The load balancer also stays internet-facing beside the API.

**Twin.** If the stem said "customers sign in with Google" instead: the same listener rule works, because a user pool also federates [Amazon, Google, Apple and Facebook](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-user-pool-workforce-sso-in-your-app).

**Takeaway.** An Application Load Balancer can sign users in through a Cognito user pool, on an HTTPS listener.

**Review.** [A user pool federates outside providers and issues its own tokens to the app](2-deep.md#a-user-pool-federates-outside-providers-and-issues-its-own-tokens-to-the-app-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 12 AWS accounts. Employees sign in to business applications through the company's external SAML 2.0 identity provider. The company also runs a mobile app for its customers. The engineers must sign in once and use the AWS CLI with short-term credentials in every account. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Use IAM Identity Center with the external identity provider as the identity source, and assign permission sets that give access to the AWS accounts.
- Use an Amazon Cognito user pool that federates with the identity providers that the users already have, and an identity pool that issues temporary AWS credentials.
- Create an IAM user with MFA and an access key for each person in each AWS account, and rotate every access key on a fixed monthly schedule.
- Create an IAM identity provider and IAM roles in every AWS account, and build a custom broker that exchanges each sign-in for temporary role credentials.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use IAM Identity Center with the external identity provider as the identity source, and assign permission sets that give access to the AWS accounts.

**Deciding phrases.** "The engineers must sign in once", "short-term credentials in every account", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The engineers are the company's workforce, and they need many accounts. With an external provider [you only federate once](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-one-point-of-federation), and IAM Identity Center [creates and manages IAM roles](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-creates-roles-per-permission-set-not-iam-users) for each permission set in each assigned account. In the AWS CLI version 2, [the CLI manages short-term credentials automatically](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-cli-v2-sign-in-short-term-credentials).

**Why not.**

- "Use an Amazon Cognito user pool that federates ...": Cognito is built for [customer identity and access management (CIAM)](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-decision-guide-ciam-for-apps-you-build) in the apps you build. The engineers need one sign-in to every account and the AWS CLI, which IAM Identity Center gives.
- "Create an IAM user with MFA and an ...": [IAM users are granted long-term credentials](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-users-get-temporary-credentials), and the stem asks for short-term credentials, so rotation does not fix the problem.
- "Create an IAM identity provider and IAM roles ...": It works, but [direct federation to each AWS account](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-wa-two-federation-approaches) repeats the provider and the roles in every account and adds a broker to build.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The app's customers must sign in with Google and upload photos to Amazon S3 with short-term credentials" instead: Amazon Cognito, because an identity pool issues [temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-user-pool-vs-identity-pool).

**Takeaway.** Employees who need many AWS accounts get IAM Identity Center with permission sets, not Amazon Cognito.

**Review.** [IAM Identity Center turns one sign-in into a role session in each account](2-deep.md#iam-identity-center-turns-one-sign-in-into-a-role-session-in-each-account-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company has a mobile app in which customers record home-repair requests. Customers already sign in to the app through an Amazon Cognito user pool, and the app sends the user pool tokens to the company's API. A new feature saves photos from the device directly to an Amazon S3 bucket with temporary credentials, and each customer's photos go under a prefix for that customer. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST securely?

- Send the user pool ID token with each Amazon S3 request, and add a bucket policy that allows requests that carry a valid token from the pool.
- Create one IAM user for the app, keep its access key in encrypted storage on each device, and allow the user to write to the bucket.
- Add a Cognito identity pool with the user pool as its provider, and give the authenticated role access to the prefix that matches each identity ID.
- Add a Cognito identity pool with the user pool as its provider, and give the authenticated role write access to every prefix in the bucket.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a Cognito identity pool with the user pool as its provider, and give the authenticated role access to the prefix that matches each identity ID.

**Deciding phrases.** "directly to an Amazon S3 bucket with temporary credentials", "a prefix for that customer", "MOST securely"

**Why.** A user pool signs customers in, and an identity pool exchanges the token for [temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-user-pool-vs-identity-pool). Each user gets an identity ID, and a policy that uses it gives each user [access to their own folder](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-identity-id-per-user-s3-folder). No AWS key ships with the app.

**Why not.**

- "Send the user pool ID token with each ...": The user pool is there to [issue JSON web tokens (JWTs)](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-user-pool-vs-identity-pool) for the app, and Amazon S3 needs AWS credentials, which an identity pool gives.
- "Create one IAM user for the app, keep ...": The IAM guide says not to embed access keys with the app, [even in encrypted storage](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-mobile-app-never-embed-access-keys), and an access key is not temporary.
- "Add a Cognito identity pool with the user ...": It works, but every signed-in customer could write into the prefixes of all other customers, which is less secure than a role that uses the identity ID.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the app calls the company's API and nothing else" instead: the user pool tokens are enough, because API Gateway accepts a call when [the supplied token is valid](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-api-gateway-cognito-user-pools-authorizer).

**Takeaway.** App users reach Amazon S3 through an identity pool, with a role scoped to each identity ID.

**Review.** [A user pool signs users in and an identity pool hands out AWS credentials](2-deep.md#a-user-pool-signs-users-in-and-an-identity-pool-hands-out-aws-credentials-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company has an Active Directory domain in its on-premises data center and a Site-to-Site VPN connection between the data center and a VPC. The company is moving several workloads to AWS. The domain controllers can be reached from the VPC. Employees must sign in to Amazon WorkSpaces with their existing AD credentials, and user accounts must remain only in the on-premises directory. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Simple AD directory in the VPC, and create a two-way trust between the Simple AD directory and the on-premises domain.
- Create an AD Connector in the VPC that points to the on-premises domain controllers, and register the directory with the AWS services that need it.
- Launch Amazon EC2 instances in the VPC as additional domain controllers of the on-premises domain, and let Active Directory replicate the whole domain to the instances.
- Create an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory in the VPC, and create a two-way forest trust between that directory and the on-premises domain.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an AD Connector in the VPC that points to the on-premises domain controllers, and register the directory with the AWS services that need it.

**Deciding phrases.** "Amazon WorkSpaces", "user accounts must remain only in the on-premises directory", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** WorkSpaces needs the employees' AD sign-in, and the accounts stay on premises. [AD Connector is a proxy service](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-is-a-proxy), and Directory Service [does not replicate any of your directory data](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-no-data-replicated). It needs a virtual private network [(VPN) connection or Direct Connect](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-needs-vpn-or-direct-connect), and the stem gives the VPN.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Simple AD directory in the VPC, ...": Simple AD [does not support multi-factor authentication (MFA), trust relationships](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-simple-ad-unsupported-features), so it cannot trust the on-premises domain.
- "Launch Amazon EC2 instances in the VPC as ...": Domain controllers on EC2 join the domain and keep its data in AWS. With AD Connector, the directory data [remains on your domain controllers](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-no-data-replicated), as the stem requires.
- "Create an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory in ...": It works, but it adds [a highly available pair of domain controllers](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-managed-ad-dc-pair-across-azs) and a second domain to operate, and no workload here needs a domain in AWS.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Amazon RDS for SQL Server databases must use Windows Authentication through a directory that AWS manages" instead: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust, because AD Connector is [not compatible with RDS SQL Server](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-not-rds-sql-server).

**Takeaway.** Users who stay in the on-premises directory and sign in to AWS applications point to AD Connector.

**Review.** [The three Directory Service options differ in where the directory runs](2-deep.md#the-three-directory-service-options-differ-in-where-the-directory-runs-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 12 AWS accounts. Employees sign in to business applications through the company's external SAML 2.0 identity provider. The company also runs a mobile app for its customers. The app's customers must sign in with Google and upload photos to Amazon S3 with short-term credentials. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Use IAM Identity Center with the external identity provider as the identity source, and assign permission sets that give access to the AWS accounts.
- Use an Amazon Cognito user pool that federates with the identity providers that the users already have, and an identity pool that issues temporary AWS credentials.
- Create an IAM user with MFA and an access key for each person in each AWS account, and rotate every access key on a fixed monthly schedule.
- Create an IAM identity provider and IAM roles in every AWS account, and build a custom broker that exchanges each sign-in for temporary role credentials.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use an Amazon Cognito user pool that federates with the identity providers that the users already have, and an identity pool that issues temporary AWS credentials.

**Deciding phrases.** "The app's customers must sign in with Google", "upload photos to Amazon S3 with short-term credentials", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The users are customers of the app, not employees. A user pool gives sign-in with customer identities from [Amazon, Google, Apple and Facebook](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-user-pool-workforce-sso-in-your-app), and an identity pool exchanges the token for AWS credentials. The app then uploads to Amazon S3 with credentials that expire, and no key is stored.

**Why not.**

- "Use IAM Identity Center with the external identity ...": IAM Identity Center serves the workforce, and Amazon Cognito is the service to [manage identities for your customer facing applications](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-cognito-is-not-an-identity-source).
- "Create an IAM user with MFA and an ...": [IAM users are granted long-term credentials](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-users-get-temporary-credentials), and the stem asks for short-term credentials for every customer.
- "Create an IAM identity provider and IAM roles ...": It works, but the IAM guide says [whenever possible, use Amazon Cognito](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-preferred-over-direct-web-identity-federation), and the broker is code to build and run.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The engineers must sign in once and use the AWS CLI with short-term credentials in every account" instead: IAM Identity Center, because [you only federate once](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-one-point-of-federation).

**Takeaway.** Customers of an app sign in through a Cognito user pool and reach AWS through an identity pool.

**Review.** [A user pool signs users in and an identity pool hands out AWS credentials](2-deep.md#a-user-pool-signs-users-in-and-an-identity-pool-hands-out-aws-credentials-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and manages workforce access with IAM Identity Center. An administrator creates a permission set that holds an AWS managed policy for read-only access. The administrator assigns the permission set to the group of auditors for one member account. Later, a security engineer reviews the IAM resources of that member account. What does the engineer find that IAM Identity Center created for this assignment?

- One IAM user for each auditor, with a console password and the read-only policy
- One IAM group for the auditors, with the read-only policy attached to the IAM group
- A resource-based policy on each resource in the account that names the auditors group
- One IAM role whose name begins with AWSReservedSSO_ and that has the read-only policy

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** One IAM role whose name begins with AWSReservedSSO_ and that has the read-only policy

**Deciding phrases.** "assigns the permission set to the group of auditors", "IAM resources of that member account"

**Why.** A permission set is [a template that you create and maintain](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-permission-set-is-policy-template). When it is assigned to an account, IAM Identity Center creates a role for it there and [attaches the policies specified in the permission set](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-permission-set-change-updates-roles). The auditors sign in to IAM Identity Center and get a session of that role.

**Why not.**

- "One IAM user for each auditor, with a ...": IAM Identity Center [does not create IAM users and groups](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-creates-roles-per-permission-set-not-iam-users); the auditors stay in its own identity store.
- "One IAM group for the auditors, with the ...": The auditors group stays in IAM Identity Center, because it [does not create IAM users and groups](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-creates-roles-per-permission-set-not-iam-users) in the accounts.
- "A resource-based policy on each resource in the ...": A permission set holds identity-based policies, and IAM Identity Center [attaches the policies specified in the permission set](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-permission-set-change-updates-roles) to a role.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the administrator later adds a policy to the permission set" instead: the same role changes, because the [corresponding IAM policies and roles are updated accordingly](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-permission-set-change-updates-roles).

**Takeaway.** A permission set becomes an IAM role in each assigned account, and IAM Identity Center [does not create IAM users and groups](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-creates-roles-per-permission-set-not-iam-users).

**Review.** [IAM Identity Center turns one sign-in into a role session in each account](2-deep.md#iam-identity-center-turns-one-sign-in-into-a-role-session-in-each-account-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company uses IAM Identity Center for access to 30 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. The identity source is an on-premises Active Directory that is connected through AD Connector. The company is moving all workforce identities to Okta. Employees must sign in to the AWS accounts with their Okta credentials, and the company wants to automate the creation of new hires in IAM Identity Center. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Keep AD Connector as the identity source, and add Okta to IAM Identity Center as a second identity source for the employees who use Okta.
- Change the identity source of IAM Identity Center to an external identity provider, and connect Okta through SAML 2.0 with the IAM Identity Center metadata.
- Create an IAM SAML identity provider for Okta in each of the 30 member accounts, and create IAM roles in each account that trust the provider.
- Connect Okta to an Amazon Cognito user pool, and set the user pool as the identity source of IAM Identity Center for all employees.
- Turn on automatic provisioning in IAM Identity Center, and configure Okta to send users and groups to the SCIM endpoint with a bearer token.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Change the identity source of IAM Identity Center to an external identity provider, and connect Okta through SAML 2.0 with the IAM Identity Center metadata.
- Turn on automatic provisioning in IAM Identity Center, and configure Okta to send users and groups to the SCIM endpoint with a bearer token.

**Deciding phrases.** "moving all workforce identities to Okta", "automate the creation of new hires", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Okta becomes the one identity source: SAML 2.0 signs employees in, and SCIM creates and updates users and groups. Identities [must be provisioned into IAM Identity Center](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-provision-before-assign) before you assign permission sets, and SCIM does that work. Plan the switch, because a new source [might remove all user and group assignments](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-change-source-may-remove-assignments).

- Okta replaces Active Directory, and with an external provider IAM Identity Center keeps [no authentication material](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-external-idp-no-passwords-stored), so Okta checks each sign-in.
- SCIM gives [automatic provisioning (synchronization) of user and group information](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-scim-automatic-provisioning), so new hires appear without manual work.

**Why not.**

- "Keep AD Connector as the identity source, and ...": IAM Identity Center connects [only one directory or one SAML 2.0 identity provider](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-one-identity-source-at-a-time) at a time.
- "Create an IAM SAML identity provider for Okta ...": It works for sign-in, but [direct federation to each AWS account](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-wa-two-federation-approaches) repeats the provider and the roles in every member account.
- "Connect Okta to an Amazon Cognito user pool, ...": Amazon Cognito is [not a supported identity source](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-cognito-is-not-an-identity-source) of IAM Identity Center.

**Twin.** If the stem said "new hires are added by hand" instead: SAML 2.0 is enough for sign-in, but each user [must be provisioned into IAM Identity Center](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-provision-before-assign) before an assignment.

**Takeaway.** An external identity provider uses SAML 2.0 for sign-in and SCIM to create users in IAM Identity Center.

**Review.** [The identity source decides where users live and who checks passwords](2-deep.md#the-identity-source-decides-where-users-live-and-who-checks-passwords-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company has one AWS account and does not use AWS Organizations. The company plans to keep this single-account setup. The company runs AWS Managed Microsoft AD in a VPC for its Windows workloads, and its ten administrators have user accounts in this directory. The administrators must use the AWS Management Console with their directory credentials. The company wants to avoid IAM users. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an IAM user for each administrator with the same name and password as in the directory, and require MFA for each IAM user.
- Enable an account instance of IAM Identity Center in the account, connect the directory, and assign permission sets to the administrators' group.
- Create an access URL for the directory, assign an IAM role to the directory group of the administrators, and let them sign in at that URL.
- Run AD FS on Amazon EC2 instances joined to the directory, create a SAML identity provider and IAM roles in the account, and federate the administrators.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an access URL for the directory, assign an IAM role to the directory group of the administrators, and let them sign in at that URL.

**Deciding phrases.** "one AWS account and does not use AWS Organizations", "with their directory credentials", "wants to avoid IAM users", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Directory members [do not have access to any AWS resources](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-console-access-iam-roles-access-url) until you give it. [You assign IAM roles to your directory members](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-console-access-iam-roles-access-url), and [your directory must have an access URL](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-console-access-iam-roles-access-url). The administrators then sign in with their directory credentials, and no IAM user exists.

**Why not.**

- "Create an IAM user for each administrator with ...": The company wants to avoid IAM users, and [IAM users are granted long-term credentials](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-users-get-temporary-credentials) that are separate from the directory passwords.
- "Enable an account instance of IAM Identity Center ...": Permission sets are [available only for organization instances](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-permission-sets-need-organization-instance), so an account instance has none to assign.
- "Run AD FS on Amazon EC2 instances joined ...": It works through IAM federation [to specific AWS accounts](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-decision-guide-federation-with-iam), but the company runs and patches its own AD FS servers, while the directory [supports federated use cases using Active Directory credentials](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-managed-ad-console-and-identity-center).

**Twin.** If the stem said "40 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations" instead: IAM Identity Center with the directory as identity source, because it gives [single sign-on to multiple AWS accounts](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-wa-two-federation-approaches).

**Takeaway.** Directory users of one account reach the console through IAM roles and the access URL of the directory.

**Review.** [Direct SAML federation works per account while Identity Center federates once](2-deep.md#direct-saml-federation-works-per-account-while-identity-center-federates-once-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs a hybrid environment. Its on-premises data center has two Active Directory forests, and AWS Direct Connect links the data center to a VPC in the AWS Organizations management account. The company uses IAM Identity Center for access to many AWS accounts. Employees from both forests must sign in to IAM Identity Center with their existing Active Directory credentials. What is the MOST operationally efficient way to meet these requirements?

- Create AWS Managed Microsoft AD in the management account, create a two-way forest trust to each forest, and set the directory as the identity source.
- Create one AD Connector for each forest in the management account, and connect both AD Connector directories to IAM Identity Center as identity sources.
- Create AWS Managed Microsoft AD in the management account, create a one-way forest trust to each forest, and set the directory as the identity source.
- Migrate the users of both forests into AWS Managed Microsoft AD with the Active Directory Migration Toolkit (ADMT), and set the directory as the identity source.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create AWS Managed Microsoft AD in the management account, create a two-way forest trust to each forest, and set the directory as the identity source.

**Deciding phrases.** "two Active Directory forests", "Employees from both forests", "MOST operationally efficient"

**Why.** AWS says to use AWS Managed Microsoft AD to [support multiple domains or forests](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-one-ad-directory-managed-ad-for-multiple-forests). IAM Identity Center [requires a two-way trust](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-needs-two-way-trust-not-one-way) to each forest. With this source, [no password information is synchronized](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-ad-pass-through-no-passwords-synced), so the passwords stay in the forests.

**Why not.**

- "Create one AD Connector for each forest in ...": IAM Identity Center can [connect only one AD Connector directory](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-one-ad-directory-managed-ad-for-multiple-forests) at a time, so two forests need another design.
- "Create AWS Managed Microsoft AD in the management ...": IAM Identity Center [requires a two-way trust](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-needs-two-way-trust-not-one-way), and [one-way trusts do not work](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-needs-two-way-trust-not-one-way) with it.
- "Migrate the users of both forests into AWS ...": It works, but it moves every user into a new domain. With two trusts, users keep their on-premises credentials, and you do not need to [synchronize users, groups, or passwords](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-extend-on-prem-ad-trust-no-sync-or-admt).

**Twin.** If the stem said "one Active Directory forest with one domain" instead: AD Connector, because it [forwards sign-in requests to your on-premises Active Directory](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-is-a-proxy) without a directory in AWS.

**Takeaway.** Several on-premises forests reach IAM Identity Center through AWS Managed Microsoft AD with two-way trusts.

**Review.** [The three Directory Service options differ in where the directory runs](2-deep.md#the-three-directory-service-options-differ-in-where-the-directory-runs-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=identity-federation-q005 -->
### Question 10

A company runs a web application whose users sign in through an Amazon Cognito user pool. The application calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway, and AWS Lambda functions run behind the API. The company must restrict the API so that it accepts requests only from users who signed in to the application. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Set the API methods to AWS_IAM authorization, create an IAM user with an access key for each customer, and sign each request to the API with that access key.
- Create a Lambda authorizer that downloads the signing keys of the user pool, validates each token in custom code, and returns an IAM policy.
- Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, and allow requests only from the IP address ranges of the users of the application.
- Create an authorizer of the COGNITO_USER_POOLS type for the user pool, enable it on the API methods, and send the user's token in the Authorization header.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an authorizer of the COGNITO_USER_POOLS type for the user pool, enable it on the API methods, and send the user's token in the Authorization header.

**Deciding phrases.** "accepts requests only from users who signed in", "LEAST development effort"

**Why.** API Gateway can check user pool tokens itself: you can [let Amazon API Gateway validate the token](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-api-gateway-validates-user-pool-token) and gate access to the API. The client signs in, sends its token, and the call succeeds when [the supplied token is valid](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-api-gateway-cognito-user-pools-authorizer). The Lambda functions receive requests from signed-in users, and the team writes no token code.

**Why not.**

- "Set the API methods to AWS_IAM authorization, create ...": [IAM users are granted long-term credentials](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-users-get-temporary-credentials), and a key for every customer adds key management and request signing to the application.
- "Create a Lambda authorizer that downloads the signing ...": It works, but the team writes and maintains token checks, although you can [let Amazon API Gateway validate the token](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-api-gateway-validates-user-pool-token) of the user pool.
- "Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the ...": An IP address does not show who signed in, and the users connect from changing networks, so the rule does not check the sign-in.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the client signs requests with identity pool credentials" instead: AWS_IAM authorization, because the users [obtain temporary credentials](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-api-gateway-aws-iam-with-identity-pool) from an identity pool.

**Takeaway.** An API Gateway REST API accepts Cognito user pool tokens through a user pool authorizer, without custom code.

**Review.** [A user pool federates outside providers and issues its own tokens to the app](2-deep.md#a-user-pool-federates-outside-providers-and-issues-its-own-tokens-to-the-app-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
